blocks.text: Between 1877 and 1900 the United States transformed from a war-torn republic into the world's leading industrial power. Railroads stitched the continent together, cities swelled with immigrants, and a handful of industrialists amassed fortunes that reshaped American life. Mark Twain called the era gilded — glittering on the surface, but corroded underneath.

New technologies — the Bessemer process, the telegraph, and the assembly of vast rail networks — let a few firms dominate entire industries. Standard Oil controlled the flow of kerosene that lit American homes; Carnegie Steel supplied the beams that raised American cities.

blocks.caption: “The Bosses of the Senate,” Joseph Keppler, Puck, 1889 (Library of Congress). Trusts tower over senators dwarfed beneath them.

blocks.text: Critics warned that this concentration of wealth threatened democracy itself. Reformers demanded regulation; the debate over the proper role of government in the economy would define American politics for a century.
“What is the chief end of man? — to get rich. In what way? — dishonestly if we can; honestly if we must.” — Mark Twain, 1871

blocks.label: Think Like a Historian
paras: Who benefited from industrial consolidation, and who bore its costs? As you read, track the winners and losers of the new economy — you will build a claim about it in your workbook.
